name: Bad Religion
label: Epitaph
lede: Forty-plus years of three-part harmony at breakneck speed, and the band that started Epitaph out of a Valley kid's bedroom.

eras.title: Three chords in the San Fernando Valley
eras.text: Four high school kids from the Valley start a band in 1980 and Brett Gurewitz turns the label he invents for them into Epitaph. Their first album is fast, cheap and only sold in the low thousands at first.

years.h: Four Valley kids start Bad Religion
years.p: [[Greg Graffin|046f8f41-f788-4da6-905d-26d1856f676d]], [[Brett Gurewitz|cd40188b-ea30-4729-bebb-e8c5091c9d02]], [[Jay Bentley|5b2bf657-acc4-476e-b2f3-a72e417accf0]] and drummer Jay Ziskrout form the band in Los Angeles, playing early shows around Orange County.

years.cap: Bad Religion in concert, House of Blues, Hollywood, California. · Wikimedia
years.h: Gurewitz starts a label to press their first record
years.p: Gurewitz founds Epitaph in Los Angeles to release the band's own music.

years.h: Bad Religion EP, the first Epitaph release
years.p: The six-song debut EP comes out on Gurewitz's new Epitaph label, with Pete Finestone taking over drums from Ziskrout as the first album gets made.

years.h: How Could Hell Be Any Worse? arrives, and Epitaph is real
years.p: The band's first album on Epitaph presents their fast, angry sound. Wikipedia reports it sold roughly 12,000 copies.
years.xp:
The record put the band's melodic, harmony-heavy hardcore on the map in Los Angeles at a time when the scene was mostly about speed and shock. Gurewitz was running the label out of his life as much as an office.

Bentley left the band in 1982, one album into its life.
play: How Could Hell Be Any Worse?

eras.title: Prog detour, rehab and a restart
eras.text: A keyboard-driven left turn, a breakup and Gurewitz's time in rehab nearly end the band, until Graffin re-forms it in 1986.

years.h: Into the Unknown: keyboards, no punk, and a wall of confusion
years.p: Graffin plays keyboards on a progressive-leaning album that sounds nothing like the band's debut, and Wikipedia reports the copies were sold out of a warehouse without the band's knowledge.
years.xp:
The album stayed out of print for more than 25 years, and Wikipedia notes it was finally reissued in Epitaph's 2010 vinyl box set (3,000 copies).

Gurewitz left the band in 1983 and entered rehab for drug addiction, according to Wikipedia.

years.h: Gurewitz leaves; the band stalls
years.p: Gurewitz exits in 1983 and goes into rehab for drug addiction, per Wikipedia, and the group temporarily stops.

years.h: The band breaks up in 1985
years.p: After a stretch with [[Greg Hetson|42351137-7257-4529-be9a-57385d9a8ac0]] of the [[Circle Jerks|22995eba-1238-4b4f-a937-ac2c5767ab9f]] on guitar, the band splits in mid-1985, per Wikipedia.

years.h: Graffin re-forms the band: Bentley, Gurewitz and Hetson all back
years.p: Graffin rebuilds Bad Religion in 1986, with Bentley returning after hesitating, Gurewitz back after rehab, plus Hetson and Finestone.

eras.title: Suffer and the rebirth
eras.text: The comeback record turns a cult LA band into the reference point for melodic hardcore, and Epitaph starts behaving like a real label.

years.h: Suffer resets the sound and sets the template
years.p: The band's first album since re-forming trades noise for tight three-part harmonies at high speed, and Wikipedia reports Trust, Maximum Rocknroll and Flipside all named it album of the year.
years.xp:
Recorded with the returned lineup of Graffin, Gurewitz, Bentley, Hetson and Finestone, it is the record fans point to when they say the band sounds like Bad Religion.

It was released on Epitaph.

years.h: No Control comes out and outsells everything before it
years.p: Released in November 1989, it becomes the band's best-selling album to that point, with more than 80,000 copies sold according to Wikipedia.
play: I Want to Conquer the World

years.h: Against the Grain passes 100,000 copies
years.p: Wikipedia lists it as the band's first 100,000 seller, and it holds the song "21st Century (Digital Boy)".

years.h: Pete Finestone leaves; Bobby Schayer takes the sticks
years.p: Drummer Pete Finestone departs in April 1991 and [[Bobby Schayer|6d35d697-620b-42ec-ab32-6721e86502e7]] replaces him.

years.h: Generator, cut nearly live at Westbeach
years.p: Wikipedia says it was recorded almost live in the enlarged Westbeach Recorders studio.

eras.title: Recipe for Hate, the Atlantic deal and Gurewitz walks
eras.text: The band hits the biggest stage of its career just as its guitarist and co-writer steps away to run the label, and Epitaph's other big band was The Offspring.

years.h: Recipe for Hate lands on the Billboard Heatseekers chart
years.p: The album, with "American Jesus" and "Struck a Nerve", debuts at No. 14 on Billboard's Heatseekers chart, per Wikipedia.

years.h: Playing L7's Rock for Choice benefit at the Palladium
years.p: The band plays L7's Rock for Choice show at the Hollywood Palladium on April 30, 1993.

years.big: The label needs him more than the band does
years.src: Wikipedia: Bad Religion · Wikipedia: Brett Gurewitz
years.h: Gurewitz quits to run Epitaph as The Offspring explode
years.p: Brett Gurewitz leaves Bad Religion in 1994 to run Epitaph full time as The Offspring's success takes off, and Brian Baker of [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]] and [[Dag Nasty|4709dd69-1034-4634-9e88-d1099453b192]] joins.
years.xp:
Wikipedia dates the departure to late 1994, before Stranger Than Fiction came out, with Baker taking over guitar. Baker had previously played in Minor Threat, Dag Nasty and Junkyard.

Epitaph's own breakthrough that year was The Offspring, which is why Gurewitz went to run the label.

years.h: Stranger Than Fiction, first for Atlantic, goes gold
years.p: Released September 1994 with a re-recorded "21st Century (Digital Boy)", it peaked at No. 87 on Billboard 200 and went gold on March 4, 1998, per Wikipedia.

eras.title: Major label years
eras.text: Baker's guitar and a run of albums on Atlantic, and the sound stays intact even as the ground shifts.

years.h: The Gray Race, produced by Ric Ocasek
years.p: Former Cars frontman Ric Ocasek produces the album, which has the minor hit "A Walk".

years.h: No Substance gets mixed reviews
years.p: Wikipedia notes critics and fans were mixed on the Atlantic-era record.

years.cap: Brian Baker (Left) with Bad Religion, 1995. · Wikimedia
years.h: Opening arenas for Blink-182 for three months
years.p: The band opens a three-month U.S. arena tour for Blink-182 in summer 2000.

years.h: The New America, produced by Todd Rundgren
years.p: Todd Rundgren, an early Graffin influence, produces the album.

years.h: Schayer leaves with a shoulder injury; Wackerman drums
years.p: Bobby Schayer exits due to a shoulder injury and [[Brooks Wackerman|422763c1-9762-4586-b2a4-0a6f54ed254e]] of [[Suicidal Tendencies|e9e2a634-984f-4c10-bf7b-7970179e1ef1]] takes over.

eras.title: Home to Epitaph
eras.text: Dropped by Atlantic, the band walks back into Epitaph and Gurewitz walks back into the band.

years.h: Atlantic drops them; Gurewitz rejoins; Epitaph is home again
years.p: After Atlantic dropped the band in 2001, Bad Religion returned to Epitaph and Gurewitz rejoined, though he has not toured since.

years.h: The Process of Belief, the first Epitaph album back
years.p: The six-piece lineup records its first Epitaph release after the Atlantic split.

years.h: The Empire Strikes First is angrier and faster
years.p: Wikipedia reports Gurewitz cited anger toward George W. Bush as a major inspiration.

years.h: Epitaph reissues the first six albums and releases Along the Way
years.p: Remastered versions of the first six studio albums come out in April 2004, alongside the documentary DVD Along the Way.

years.h: New Maps of Hell becomes their biggest chart album
years.p: It reaches No. 35 on Billboard 200, which was their highest position at that time, and the band joined the 2007 Warped Tour.

eras.title: Forty years on
eras.text: Anniversary tours, a first top-20 album, a Christmas record, lineup turnover and a return to political anger.

years.h: 30 Shows in 30 Nights at the House of Blues
years.p: In March-April 2010 the band marks its 30th anniversary with 30 nights at House of Blues venues in Southern California and Nevada.

years.h: The Dissent of Man
years.p: Debuts at No. 35 on Billboard 200 and No. 6 on the Independent Albums chart, per Wikipedia.

years.h: Graffin publishes Anarchy Evolution
years.p: Greg Graffin publishes his book about faith, science and Bad Religion; he holds a PhD in evolutionary biology.

years.h: Headlining the Reason Rally in Washington, D.C.
years.p: On March 24, 2012 the band headlines the rally alongside Richard Dawkins, Tim Minchin, James Randi and Eddie Izzard.

years.h: True North is their first top-20 album
years.p: It reaches No. 18 on Billboard 200, their first top 20 in 34 years, per Wikipedia.

years.h: Greg Hetson steps back; Mike Dimkich joins
years.p: Hetson steps away from touring in May 2013; Mike Dimkich fills in and is confirmed permanent in January 2014.

years.h: Christmas Songs
years.p: The band's first Christmas album, and the first without Hetson since 1983.

years.h: Brooks Wackerman leaves for Avenged Sevenfold
years.p: Wackerman departs on October 27, 2015 and Jamie Miller takes over drums.

years.h: Age of Unreason
years.p: The seventeenth album, out May 3, 2019, is driven by the band's disdain for Donald Trump.

years.h: Do What You Want tells the band's story
years.p: The band's authorised autobiography is published August 18, 2020; COVID-19 cancels all tour dates, their first year without performances since 1980.
